newsitem.title: USA: Airports face major adjustments from cargo reforms.
newsitem.headline: Airports face major adjustments from cargo reforms.

text.p: The radical reforms being contemplated by the traditional air freight industry to meet the threat from integrated carriers will make or break airport warehouse operators around the world, says an industry automation expert.

Billions of dollars in airport warehousing facilities stand to become affected if the airlines and freight forwarders succeed in their reform drive called Cargo 2000, says Hugh Doyle, Dublin-based managing director, freight management, for Unisys Corp.

Cargo 2000, launched here this week at the Internatinonal Air Transport Association Cargo Week 97, is a joint initiative of the airline and freight forwarding industries to speed up cargo flows by streamlining processes and eliminating redundancies.

If they do not accelerate the system, the airlines will surely lose much of the world's air cargo business to integrated carriers like FedEx that can move it a lot faster, Cargo Week attendees were told.

The most obvious way to accelerate the flow and reduce cost is to move freight through airports as quickly as possible rather than warehousing it for hours or days, a function which adds cost but no customer value, Doyle told Reuters.
Government-regulated terminal monopolies may not be able to adjust to such a fundamental change, he said. They likely will disappear as part of a general lowering of impediments to free markets.
On the other hand, large, private warehouse owners have billions of dollars invested in facilities at large airports such Singapore and Hong Kong.
Initially, these operators may also fear these reforms, said Doyle.

However, without acceleration of cargo flow, prospects for the conventional air freight industry are bleak, he said. With acceleration, airlines will hold or increase their share of a fast growing global freight market.
"As soon as they (warehouse operators) realize that this business is going to treble, they will be very happy to convert their warehousing activity to a very high speed conduit facility," said Doyle.
A Unisys survey last year concluded that the average air freight shipment takes six days to move from shipper to consignee and is warehoused eight times along the way for varying periods.
Unisys concluded that integrators move it in half the time. -Air Cargo Newsroom Tel:+44 171 542 7706 Fax:5017
